extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor theory; cognitive psychologists and linguists studying humor
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for explaining and predicting humor perception/production based on Veatch's moral-affective theory of humor (distinguishing a 'normal' view N and a subjective moral 'violation' view V). Focus is on what makes situations/jokes funny or offensive across verbal and nonverbal phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity of N and V interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: The present theory says that situations in which the two views, N and V, are not simultaneously juxtaposed in the mind of the perceiver are not funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central necessary condition: both a 'normal' (N) interpretation and a subjective moral 'violation' (V) interpretation of the same situation must be present at the same time in the perceiver's mind. If the two interpretations enter and leave sequentially without overlap, humor will not occur. Timing and delivery must therefore engineer temporal overlap of the two interpretations. Repetition, which removes surprise and allows settling on a single interpretation, reduces the chance of simultaneity and thus reduces funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective component: moral/subjective violation vs normality (V vs N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor involves one view of the situation being a moral or affectively significant violation (V) and another view being normal (N); the V interpretation depends on the perceiver caring about the principle violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perceived violation must concern something the perceiver has emotional commitment to; strength of that commitment affects whether a situation is funny, offensive, or neither. The V interpretation is not merely cognitive inconsistency but an affective judgment about how things ought to be. This explains differences across audiences and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: brevity and surprise facilitate humor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Brevity is the soul of wit" — if elements are presented quickly, N and V are more likely to overlap; surprise enables sudden juxtaposition of interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity increases temporal overlap of interpretations; surprise can produce a brief interval where both views coexist (thereby enabling humor). Surprise is not necessary nor sufficient (many surprises aren't funny, and some humor lacks surprise), but it often functions as an enabling factor. Repetition reduces surprise and can make jokes less funny because it removes the transient overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension difficulty (optimal, inverted-U effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived humor increases as comprehension difficulty increases up to a point, then decreases as difficulty becomes too high (Wyer & Collins' finding, accommodated here via timing/simultaneity effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate difficulty can prolong the presence of the first interpretation until the second is found, helping simultaneity; too difficult prevents finding the second interpretation (no humor), too easy means the first interpretation is not sufficiently convincing (no humor) or the listener settles on a single interpretation. Thus an intermediate level of interpretive difficulty maximizes humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive restructuring: expectation and alternative view must both make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Gleitman's 'cognitive restructuring' elements map to N and V: an expectation is built and then fails but the surprising outcome also 'makes sense' — both views are coherent interpretations of the same situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the original expectation and the violating interpretation must be plausible ways of making sense of the situation. However, cognitive expectation alone is insufficient; the affective/moral attachment to the expectation (the V/N distinction) is required for humor according to the present theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggression as a possible but insufficient explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggression-based theories (humor as aggression) can be interpreted as consistent with moments when humor involves taking pleasure in another's error, but they are inadequate because humor can be non-aggressive and often has ameliorative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggression may explain some cases (latent or manifest pleasure at another's fault), but it fails to account for many facts predicted by the present moral-affective theory (e.g., simultaneity requirement, normalizing function). Do not treat aggression as the primary criterion; consider it a related consequence in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority as a consequence, not a necessary condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings of superiority (Hobbes) occur when someone else is responsible for a moral violation and the perceiver is not, enabling the perceiver to feel superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superiority often follows from N/V configurations where the perceiver is not the violator; it helps explain many instances of laughter directed at others. However, superiority is not necessary for all humor (self-directed humor can be analyzed but requires conceptualizing two selves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief laughter / peekaboo: humor from reestablishment of normality
rubrics_metrics.description: When something initially seems badly wrong and then turns out to be okay, laughter (relief) often occurs; in infants this links to object permanence stage 2 (disappearance interpreted as nonexistence then reappearance is relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief humor depends on a transient V interpretation (loss/nonexistence) that is undone. Intensity and duration matter: too long a disappearance or too strong an attachment (e.g., mother's absence) yields crying, not laughter. Developmental stage shapes whether peekaboo is amusing (stage 2) or not (stage 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Giggle-fest / contagious laughter as social following rather than cognitive humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Group laughter can spread contagiously; joiners may laugh without cognitively perceiving humor — it's a social following behavior like yawning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume contagious laughter always signals comprehension of an N/V juxtaposition; it may be driven by social mimicry or affective contagion. A theory of humor perception need not explain contagion fully; treat it as part of broader social following mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic humor counted via sociolinguistic evaluative commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic violations (puns, grammatical errors, dialect mimicry) can be humorously evaluated because people have affective attachments to linguistic 'propriety' and judge linguistic misbehavior as violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent counterexamples (language-as-purely-cognitive) are accommodated by recognizing cultural/sociolinguistic norms: speakers make evaluative judgments about language form and thereby can experience V interpretations. Consider prescriptive attitudes (e.g., reactions to nonstandard forms) as affective commitments that enable humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns: mild moral violation via logical inconsistency plus ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns often combine a mild moral violation (faulty or blatantly inconsistent reasoning) with a 'straight' interpretation via ambiguity; this yields an ambiguous, usually weak humorous response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns typically produce groans or mild amusement rather than strong laughter. The structure: an ambiguous phrase allows a path of apparently legitimate reasoning (normal) that coexists with a clearly inconsistent claim (violation). The social failure of the pun performance (e.g., 'that's terrible') can itself be the source of humor in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness determined by degree of moral commitment and interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a joke is offensive or funny depends on whether listeners can construe a 'normal' interpretation alongside the violating interpretation and on how strongly they are committed to the violated principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an audience cannot grant a normal reading (due to high moral commitment or poor delivery), the V interpretation dominates and the joke is likely offensive or simply unacceptable. Universally held moral principles (sanctity of life, religious devotion) increase likelihood of offense. Delivery and context can modulate perceived offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set jokes and context dependence: need for non-textual and subject differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal/joke-text theories (e.g., Raskin) are limited to textual compatibility with two semantic scripts; a fuller account must handle non-linguistic humor and differences across subjects/situations where context or affective evaluations change outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze jokes with attention to extra-textual factors (situation, perceiver's affective commitments, social tension). Do not restrict evaluation to formal textual properties; include audience-specific and situational variables that affect whether N and V readings are available and simultaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: all humor phenomena map to N/V analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of phenomena (inebriation, satire, satire, exaggeration, ridicule, embarrassment, slapstick, puns, peekaboo, relief laughter, giggle-fests) can be explained by mapping them onto the normal (N) vs subjective moral violation (V) framework plus timing and affective commitment factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a humor instance, identify (a) what counts as the N interpretation, (b) what counts as the V interpretation and why it matters to perceivers, (c) whether both interpretations are temporally co-present, and (d) audience/contextual factors (commitment strength, development, social following). Use these axes to predict funniness, offensiveness, or lack of humor.
